headline: AIPAC announces it will stop officially endorsing candidates and making direct PAC contributions
dek: AIPAC announced Wednesday it will no longer issue official endorsements of congressional candidates, make direct campaign contributions through its PAC, or channel member donations (earmarking). It will continue operating its United Democracy Project super PAC and pivot to mobilizing direct…
sources: AIPAC board letter to members (signed by president Bernie Kaminetsky et al); spokesperson Deryn Sousa to Jewish Insider/NPR/Haaretz; NPR Saige Miller; Haaretz
fault_line: Is the most powerful pro-Israel lobby retreating because it lost the public (Gaza/Iran wars backlash) — or just laundering the same money through the super PAC?

sections.what_happened: AIPAC announced Wednesday it will no longer issue official endorsements of congressional candidates, make direct campaign contributions through its PAC, or channel member donations (earmarking). It will continue operating its United Democracy Project super PAC and pivot to mobilizing direct individual giving ('more than $90M directly to candidates this cycle' per Sousa). The move returns AIPAC to its pre-2021 model after ~5 years of direct endorsement politics; stated reason: its backing has become a political liability as candidates face backlash from both right and left over accepting AIPAC support (wars in Gaza and Iran cited by NPR).
sections.what_verified: NPR, Haaretz, Washington Sun, Jewish Insider all carry the board letter and Sousa quotes
sections.what_disputed: n/a — this is a retreat from endorsements, not a withdrawal from spending; TYT's 'Down Goes AIPAC?' framing overstates the move
sections.why_matters: The retreat is the story: after five years of direct endorsement politics, AIPAC's brand became a liability candidates refuse to touch — a hard indicator of how far US public opinion has moved against the wars. Frame: what changed in American politics, not the gossip.
sections.context: Background: US politics — NEW (Oct 21): AIPAC announces it will stop officially endorsing candidates and making direct PAC contributions

totw_analysis: Our read: The retreat is the story: after five years of direct endorsement politics, AIPAC's brand became a liability candidates refuse to touch — a hard indicator of how far US public opinion has moved against the wars. Frame: what changed in American politics, not the gossip. The fault line our audience is arguing over: Is the most powerful pro-Israel lobby retreating because it lost the public (Gaza/Iran wars backlash) — or just laundering the same money through the super PAC?
